transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because… for about the past year, I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. Everyone keeps telling me the numbers are fine—doctors, my family—but I know what I saw, and the chart doesn’t match. It’s just been wearing me down.
Besides this concern about your dad's lab results, have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people around you don't seem to hear or see?
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t heard voices or seen things like that. It’s more about the records and what I saw in the chart.
Do you have any medical conditions—such as a head injury, seizures, thyroid problems, or use of drugs or alcohol—that started around the same time these concerns about your dad's records began?

Not that I know of. I mean, I don’t have anything like that that started around then. I don’t really use drugs, and alcohol isn’t a big thing for me. I haven’t noticed some medical problem that lines up with when this started.

Aside from this concern about your dad’s records, has your day-to-day functioning—like your work, your ability to take care of yourself, or your relationships with other people—changed or gotten harder over this past year?

Outside of the whole thing with my dad’s records, I’d say I’m still functioning. I keep my phlebotomy shifts, I pay my bills, I take care of myself. I’m still managing the normal day-to-day stuff. It’s really this one issue that’s been taking up so much of my attention.
If your dad's doctors showed you the original lab reports and explained the process in detail, is there anything they could show you that would convince you the records weren't altered?

Honestly, I don’t know what would convince me at this point. If they showed me something now, I’d still wonder if it was the “original” or just what they want me to see.

I know my family and the doctors keep saying the numbers are fine, but I know what I saw in the chart before, and it doesn’t match. That’s why I’ve been trying for the past year to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing something or holding parts back. It’s exhausting, but I can’t just ignore it.

Aside from this concern about your dad's records, do you find yourself suspicious or distrustful of other people or institutions in your life—like coworkers, neighbors, or organizations you deal with?

Not really, no. I mean, I deal with people at work and I don’t feel like everyone is out to get me or anything. I don’t have problems with my neighbors or other places I deal with. This is really about my dad’s records and that clinic system.

Over this past year, have you noticed any significant changes in your mood—like feeling persistently sad, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually elevated, energetic, or needing much less sleep than usual?

I haven’t really noticed anything like that. I mean, I get stressed and worn out from dealing with this, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been persistently sad or unusually energized or anything like that. My mood feels mostly like my normal mood, just frustrated.
Have you noticed any trouble organizing your thoughts, or has anyone told you that your speech seems disjointed or hard to follow?
No, I don’t think so. I feel like I can explain what I mean pretty clearly, even if people don’t agree with me. Nobody’s told me I’m hard to follow or anything like that.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, well-circumscribed, non-bizarre delusion (belief that clinic staff are altering/withholding her father's lab results) persisting for about one year. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech, no negative symptoms, and no mood episode symptoms (depressive or manic). Functioning is preserved outside the delusional theme—she maintains her job, self-care, and finances. The delusion is encapsulated (not part of a broader pattern of paranoia toward others) and she is not fully convinced by contrary evidence but can articulate her reasoning coherently. This clinical picture is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22) rather than Schizophrenia (which requires additional psychotic symptoms and functional decline) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (no mood symptoms present).
